what_it_does: Traditional servers pack all computing components — processor, memory, storage, and network card — into one box. 'Disaggregated' architectures instead split these into separate, independently managed units connected by a high-speed network, allowing data centers to mix and match resources more flexibly. This invited position paper argues that splitting things up this way opens new security risks: data crossing network links can be intercepted or tampered with, different tenants' workloads may 'see' each other's data, and software-defined radio networks (called O-RAN — open, software-controlled mobile network infrastructure) introduce their own vulnerabilities. The authors survey attack surfaces across three real-world domains — enterprise networking, O-RAN, and secure isolated computing environments (areas of a chip that are walled off from the rest of the system to protect sensitive code) — and outline open challenges rather than proposing a single solution.
